kurals.tamil:
நடுவின்றி நன்பொருள் வெஃகின் குடிபொன்றிக்
குற்றமும் ஆங்கே தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Naduvindri nanporul vehkin kudiponrik
Kutramum aange tharum.
kurals.meaning: If a person abandons fairness and sets his heart on the good property that belongs to someone else, that very desire will bring ruin on his family and guilt on himself, right then and there.
kurals.elementary: Imagine wanting your classmate’s new bike so badly that you stop caring what is fair. This kural says that kind of wanting is like a crack in your own house: it doesn’t just get you in trouble, it hurts your whole family too.
kurals.university: The chapter opens with its thesis in its strongest form: covetousness (வெஃகுதல், vehkuthal) is condemned not only as an act of seizure but as a desire born of abandoning நடு (nadu), the equity or impartiality Valluvar had already exalted in chapter 12 (நடுவு நிலைமை). The consequences are twofold and immediate: the family line (குடி, kudi) is destroyed and guilt (குற்றம்) accrues, and the word ஆங்கே (aange, “right there, at that moment”) insists that the damage is not deferred to a future birth but arrives simultaneously with the desire. Parimelazhagar reads the kural as addressed to the householder, which explains why the penalty falls on the kudi: the covetous man betrays the very household he is supposed to sustain. The idea that injustice in acquisition corrodes the acquirer’s own house recurs across traditions, from the Hebrew story of Achan to Aristotle’s analysis of pleonexia as a vice of unfairness (anisotes).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Duryodhana, consumed by desire for the kingdom and wealth that rightfully belonged to his Pandava cousins, refused even a compromise of five villages. The war that followed at Kurukshetra annihilated his entire line of brothers, sons, and allies.
hinduism.explanation: Duryodhana coveted what was not his, ignored every appeal to fairness, and in the end his whole family was wiped out in the war he started to keep it.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says unfair coveting destroys one’s own kudi (family line); the Mahabharata is the epic-scale illustration of exactly that.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva and Stri Parva (narrative)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel (covetousness of another’s rightful property leading to the destruction of one’s own clan); paraphrased summary of a long narrative, not a direct quote.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns Timothy that the very desire to get rich is a trap that leads people into ruin.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it locates the danger in the desire itself and says it ends in destruction.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (KJV). Matches desire-leads-to-destruction; lacks the Kural’s specific emphasis on another’s property and on the family’s ruin.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly but only [in lawful] business by mutual consent.” … “And whoever does that in aggression and injustice - then We will drive him into a Fire.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids taking other people’s wealth unfairly and warns of punishment for doing it out of injustice.
islam.tie_back: “Unjustly” is the Qur’anic equivalent of the Kural’s naduvindri (without fairness), and both attach guilt to it.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (Sahih International). Strong on the unjust-taking-of-others’-wealth element and on resulting guilt; does not mention ruin of the family.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When I saw among the spoils a goodly Babylonish garment, and two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold of fifty shekels weight, then I coveted them, and took them.”
judaism.explanation: Achan confesses that he saw forbidden treasure, coveted it, and hid it in his tent. The narrative then records that he was executed together with his sons, daughters, livestock, and tent (Joshua 7:24-25).
judaism.tie_back: Almost a narrative enactment of the Kural: covet what is not yours, and your whole household is destroyed along with you.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (KJV). Close structural match: coveting another’s (here God-devoted) property leads to the destruction of the coveter’s household.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Riches ruin only the foolish, not those in quest of the Beyond. By craving for riches the witless man ruins himself as well as others.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that craving for wealth destroys not only the person who craves but also the people around him.
buddhism.tie_back: Same double damage as the Kural: the coveter harms himself and those connected to him.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Matches craving-ruins-self-and-others; speaks of craving for riches generally rather than for another’s property specifically.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Eriphyle, bribed with the golden necklace of Harmonia, sent her husband Amphiaraus to his death in the expedition against Thebes; her son Alcmaeon later killed her in revenge. Homer names her among the shades in the underworld as the woman who took gold as the price of her own husband.
greek_mythology.explanation: One woman’s desire for a precious necklace that was not hers set off a chain of death and revenge that destroyed her own family.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Covetousness for a “good thing” (nanporul) led directly to the ruin of the household, just as the Kural warns.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Odyssey 11 (Eriphyle among the shades); fuller story in later mythographers
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Homer only alludes briefly; the full murder-and-revenge narrative is from later tradition (e.g., Apollodorus).

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle defines the unjust man in the particular sense as “grasping” (pleonektes) and “unfair” (anisos): one who takes more than his share of goods at the expense of others.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, the vice of wanting more than your fair share is precisely what injustice is, and it is a defect of character, not just a bad act.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s link between grasping and unfairness mirrors the Kural’s link between coveting and loss of nadu (equity).
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Aristotle’s argument. Excellent conceptual match on covetousness-as-unfairness; Aristotle does not speak of family ruin.

kurals.tamil:
படுபயன் வெஃகிப் பழிப்படுவ செய்யார்
நடுவன்மை நாணு பவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Padupayan vehkip pazhippaduva seyyaar
Naduvanmai naanu pavar.
kurals.meaning: People who feel shame at the very idea of being unfair will never do disgraceful things just because they want the profit they could get from them.
kurals.elementary: Suppose you could win a game by quietly peeking at someone’s cards. A person who would feel embarrassed to cheat just won’t do it, even if it means winning. This kural says that feeling of shame protects you from doing wrong for a prize.
kurals.university: Where kural 171 threatened consequences, 172 names the internal safeguard: நாண் (naan), a moral sense of shame or modesty, here specifically shame at நடுவன்மை (naduvanmai, “non-equity”). The phrase படுபயன் (padupayan) denotes the gain that “falls” to one, the benefit that would accrue from taking another’s property, and பழிப்படுவ (pazhippaduva) are acts that incur public blame. Valluvar’s psychology is notable: the person of integrity is restrained less by fear of punishment than by an internalised aversion to injustice, a theme developed fully in chapter 102 (நாணுடைமை). This aligns with Gita ethics, in which modesty (Sanskrit hri) and the reflex of weighing gain against righteousness are marks of a mature moral agent.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…compassion and freedom from covetousness; gentleness, modesty and steady determination … these transcendental qualities, O son of Bharata, belong to godly men endowed with divine nature.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists the qualities of a divinely-natured person; two of them are freedom from covetousness (aloluptvam) and modesty, or a sense of shame at wrongdoing (hri).
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural pairs the same two things: shame at wrongdoing, and therefore no coveting.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (excerpted). Strong conceptual pairing of hri (shame/modesty) and aloluptvam (non-covetousness); a list rather than a causal statement.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not be once named among you, as becometh saints.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers that covetousness is so unfitting for holy people that it should not even be mentioned among them.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts appeal to a sense of what is fitting or shameful: good people recoil from covetousness itself.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Shares the propriety/shame framing against covetousness; lacks the specific ‘for the sake of gain’ logic.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly or send it [in bribery] to the rulers in order that [they might aid] you [to] consume a portion of the wealth of the people in sin, while you know [it is unlawful].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids scheming, including bribery, to get other people’s wealth, noting that people do this even while knowing it is wrong.
islam.tie_back: The Kural says the person with a conscience will not do blameworthy deeds for profit; the Qur’an names exactly those blameworthy schemes and forbids them.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Good match on disgraceful acts done for gain; the shame motive is implicit (‘while you know’) rather than explicit.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Behold, here I am: witness against me before the LORD, and before his anointed: whose ox have I taken? or whose ass have I taken? or whom have I defrauded? whom have I oppressed? or of whose hand have I received any bribe to blind mine eyes therewith?”
judaism.explanation: At the end of his career Samuel publicly challenges the people to name anything he took unjustly; no one can.
judaism.tie_back: Samuel is the portrait of the person the Kural describes: someone so ashamed of injustice that he never profited from it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. A lived example of refusing gain through injustice; the shame motive is inferred rather than stated.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He is indeed virtuous, wise, and righteous who neither for his own sake nor for the sake of another (does any wrong), who does not crave for sons, wealth, or kingdom, and does not desire success by unjust means.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha defines the righteous person as someone who will not seek wealth or success through unjust means.
buddhism.tie_back: Nearly the Kural’s statement: the righteous person does not pursue gain through injustice.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Close match on refusing unjust gain; the shame/naan element is absent.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Do not get base gain: base gain is as bad as ruin.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns his brother that dishonest profit is no profit at all; it is equivalent to disaster.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural says the honourable will not do blameworthy deeds for gain; Hesiod gives the same rule in one line.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (Theoi/Evelyn-White). Direct parallel on refusing disgraceful gain; framed as prudence, not shame.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Now, suppose a wise man had just such a ring, he would not imagine that he was free to do wrongly any more than if he did not have it; for good men aim to secure not secrecy but the right.”
philosophy.explanation: Retelling Plato’s story of Gyges’ ring of invisibility, Cicero argues that a good person would not use a guarantee of impunity to take what is not his, because what restrains him is the wrongness of the act and not fear of being found out.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s inner safeguard: the person who is ashamed of injustice turns down disgraceful gain even when nothing outside him would stop him.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis (On Duties), Book III, §38 (tr. Walter Miller (Loeb, 1913))
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on LacusCurtius (De Officiis III.35-95, Miller). Strong match on restraint grounded in internal moral sense rather than fear of consequences; Cicero speaks of a commitment to the right rather than naming shame (naan) specifically.

kurals.tamil:
சிற்றின்பம் வெஃகி அறனல்ல செய்யாரே
மற்றின்பம் வேண்டு பவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Sitrinbam vehki aranalla seyyaare
Matrinbam vendu pavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who seek the other, lasting joy will never do unrighteous things just to grab a small, passing pleasure.
kurals.elementary: If you are saving your pocket money for something you really love, you won’t spend it on a cheap sweet that’s gone in a minute. This kural says people who want the big, lasting kind of happiness don’t do bad things for tiny, quick treats.
kurals.university: The kural sets up a contrast between சிற்றின்பம் (sitrinbam, “petty pleasure”) and மற்றின்பம் (matrinbam, “the other joy”). Parimelazhagar glosses the latter as the bliss of heaven or liberation, while modern commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan read it as the enduring happiness that flows from aram (virtue); either way, the argument is a rational trade-off, not a prohibition. Covetousness is foolish because it sacrifices a greater, lasting good for a trivial, fleeting one. This is among the most widely shared structures in world ethics: the Buddha’s ‘renounce the lesser happiness for the greater’, Nachiketas refusing Death’s riches, and Socrates rebuking Athens for preferring money to the soul all have the same shape.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “These things last till tomorrow, O Death, for they wear out this vigour of all the senses.” … “No man can be made happy by wealth.”
hinduism.explanation: When Death offers the boy Nachiketas cattle, gold, long life, and a kingdom to stop him asking about the Self, Nachiketas refuses: such pleasures do not last and cannot truly satisfy.
hinduism.tie_back: Nachiketas is the Kural’s model: he wants the ‘other joy’ and so will not trade it for small, passing pleasures.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (Müller, SBE 15). Very close match on rejecting fleeting wealth for lasting good; the element of unrighteous means is not present.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts earthly treasure, which decays and can be stolen, with heavenly treasure, which lasts.
christianity.tie_back: Same contrast of a perishable lesser good against an imperishable greater one.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Strong on the lesser-versus-lasting contrast; does not address wrongdoing to obtain the lesser good.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not extend your eyes toward that by which We have given enjoyment to [some] categories of them, [its being but] the splendor of worldly life by which We test them. And the provision of your Lord is better and more enduring.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells the believer not to look longingly at the worldly enjoyments of others, because God’s provision is better and lasts longer.
islam.tie_back: An almost exact match: don’t covet others’ passing pleasures, because the other joy is better and more enduring.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Near one-to-one: covetous gazing at others’ enjoyments versus a better, more enduring good.

judaism.quote_or_event: “More precious is one hour in repentance and good deeds in this world, than all the life of the world to come; And more precious is one hour of the tranquility of the world to come, than all the life of this world.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah weighs this world’s pleasures against the world to come, and says one hour of that tranquility outweighs a whole lifetime here.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it measures worldly pleasure against a far greater joy that makes the smaller one not worth sinning for.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (Sefaria, Kulp translation). Good match on lesser versus greater joy; does not mention coveting.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If by renouncing a lesser happiness one may realize a greater happiness, let the wise man renounce the lesser, having regard for the greater.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the wise to give up small pleasures when doing so leads to a far greater happiness.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s sitrinbam/matrinbam argument almost word for word.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Near one-to-one structural match (lesser happiness versus greater happiness).

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Stranded on Thrinacia, Odysseus’ starving crew ignored his warning and slaughtered the sacred cattle of Helios for a feast. Zeus destroyed their ship and every one of them lost the homecoming they had struggled ten years to reach.
greek_mythology.explanation: The sailors took something that was not theirs for a few days of feasting and lost their lives and their return home.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They traded the ‘other joy’ (homecoming) for a petty, unlawful pleasure, exactly what the Kural says the wise never do.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the episode. Strong narrative match: unlawful appropriation for a short-lived pleasure costs the greater good.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “O my friend, why do you who are a citizen of the great and mighty and wise city of Athens, care so much about laying up the greatest amount of money and honor and reputation, and so little about wisdom and truth and the greatest improvement of the soul?”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates tells his jury that he spends his life challenging people who chase money while neglecting the soul.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates, like Valluvar, calls it a bad trade to chase lesser goods at the expense of the greater one.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (MIT Classics, Jowett), trimmed at the end of the sentence. Strong on lesser-versus-greater good; does not address unrighteous acquisition.

kurals.tamil:
இலமென்று வெஃகுதல் செய்யார் புலம்வென்ற
புன்மையில் காட்சி யவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ilamendru vehkuthal seyyaar pulamvendra
Punmaiyil kaatchi yavar.
kurals.meaning: People of flawless insight who have mastered their senses will not covet what belongs to others, not even when they think, “We are poor and have nothing.”
kurals.elementary: It is easy not to want your friend’s lunch when you already have a big one. This kural is about someone who is really hungry and still doesn’t take what isn’t theirs, because they’ve trained themselves to be strong inside.
kurals.university: This kural removes the most sympathetic excuse for covetousness: need. இலம் என்று (ilam endru, “saying ‘we have nothing’”) captures the self-justifying thought of the poor, and Valluvar insists that even this does not license desire for another’s goods among those who are புலம் வென்ற (pulam venra, “sense-conquered”) and of புன்மையில் காட்சி (punmaiyil kaatchi, “vision free from meanness”). The pairing of sense-mastery with non-covetousness is characteristically Indian (compare the Gita’s sthitaprajna), but the insistence that integrity must survive poverty is universal, as Agur’s prayer in Proverbs attests. Valluvar is not romanticising poverty; he is arguing that virtue that fails under pressure was never virtue.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is able to withdraw his senses from sense objects, as the tortoise draws his limbs within the shell, is to be understood as truly situated in knowledge.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the steady-minded sage as someone who can pull his senses back from their objects the way a tortoise pulls in its limbs.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s pulam venra (sense-conquered) person is exactly this tortoise-like sage, who is not pulled toward others’ goods even in want.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Matches the sense-mastery half; the poverty context and covetousness are not in the verse.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound … both to abound and to suffer need.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says he has learned to be content whether he has plenty or is going without.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s sage, Paul’s contentment doesn’t collapse when he is poor.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Strong match on contentment in need; coveting others’ goods is implied rather than explicit.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Charity is] for the poor who have been restricted for the cause of Allah … An ignorant [person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint … They do not ask people persistently [or at all].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises poor people whose self-restraint is so great that outsiders think they are well-off, since they do not press others for what they have.
islam.tie_back: These are the Kural’s people: genuinely poor, yet with such restraint that they reach for nothing that belongs to others.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (excerpted). Strong on restraint in poverty; about not begging rather than not coveting, a close cousin.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me: Lest I be full, and deny thee … or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain.”
judaism.explanation: Agur asks God to spare him from poverty precisely because he knows poverty tempts people to take what isn’t theirs.
judaism.tie_back: Proverbs names the very temptation the Kural addresses (poverty as an excuse to take), though it asks to be spared the test instead of praising those who pass it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (excerpted). Same situation (poverty tempting toward theft), but a prayer to avoid it rather than a portrait of the one who resists.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Health is the most precious gain and contentment the greatest wealth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says contentment itself is the greatest wealth, so someone who has it is never truly poor.
buddhism.tie_back: This is why the Kural’s sage does not covet even in want: his real wealth is his contentment.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (first half of the verse). Supplies the underlying rationale; does not address sense-mastery or coveting directly.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Fools! They know not how much more the half is than the whole, nor what great advantage there is in mallow and asphodel.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod mocks greedy men who don’t realise that a modest share, even the poor man’s simple food of mallow and asphodel, is worth more than grabbing everything.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both texts honour the person who can live on little without reaching for more.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Praises contentment with poor fare against greed; not specifically about resisting temptation in poverty.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Not even the impudence of my accusers dares to say that I have ever exacted or sought pay of anyone; they have no witness of that. And I have a witness of the truth of what I say; my poverty is a sufficient witness.”
philosophy.explanation: At his trial Socrates points to his own poverty as proof that, despite years of teaching, he never took money from anyone, and he had earlier said he lived in utter poverty because of his devotion to the god.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates is the Kural’s person of clear vision who stays poor but does not reach for what is not his.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim at MIT Internet Classics Archive (Jowett). Strong example of integrity kept in poverty; the parallel is to refusing fees rather than to coveting another person's property, and the Kural's sense-mastery theme is absent. Quote begins mid-sentence ('...but now, as you will perceive, not even...'); the capital 'N' is editorial.

kurals.tamil:
அஃகி அகன்ற அறிவென்னாம் யார்மாட்டும்
வெஃகி வெறிய செயின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ahki akandra arivennaam yaarmaattum
Vehki veriya seyin.
kurals.meaning: What good is a mind that is both sharp and broad, if its owner covets other people’s things and behaves senselessly toward anyone at all?
kurals.elementary: Imagine the smartest kid in class who uses their brains to trick friends out of their toys. Being clever doesn’t make that okay; it just makes the cleverness useless. This kural says being smart means nothing if greed makes you act foolishly.
kurals.university: The first line is a small masterpiece of sound and sense: அஃகி அகன்ற அறிவு (ahki akandra arivu) describes knowledge that is at once narrowed to a fine point (ahku, ‘to become subtle/minute’) and broadened (akal, ‘to spread wide’), in other words both deep and wide. The rhetorical question ‘என்னாம்?’ (ennaam, ‘of what use?’) then cancels that learning entirely if its possessor, driven by covetousness, does வெறிய (veriya, senseless or improper deeds) toward யார்மாட்டும் (yaarmaattum, ‘anyone whatsoever’). The kural anticipates the chapter on learning (40-43) by insisting that intellect is not a moral safeguard; covetousness can hijack it. The Gita’s chain of desire, anger, delusion, and ‘loss of intelligence’ and Plato’s image of reason enslaved to money-making make the same diagnosis.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “From anger, delusion arises, and from delusion bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, intelligence is lost, and when intelligence is lost, one falls down again into the material pool.”
hinduism.explanation: Continuing the previous verse (2.62, where attachment breeds desire and desire breeds anger), Krishna traces how unchecked desire ends by destroying the intellect itself.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s point exactly: however great your intelligence, covetous desire can make it useless.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Strong psychological match (desire leading to loss of buddhi); the chain begins with desire generally, not coveting others’ goods specifically.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says that even total knowledge is worth nothing without love.
christianity.tie_back: Same rhetorical structure as the Kural (‘what use is all knowledge if…?’), although Paul’s condition is lack of love rather than presence of greed.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Matches the ‘knowledge is worthless without virtue’ structure; covetousness is not the named failing.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of those who were entrusted with the Torah and then did not take it on is like that of a donkey who carries volumes [of books].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an compares people who carry knowledge but do not live by it to a donkey loaded with books it cannot use.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it declares learning useless when conduct contradicts it.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Best available match on ‘knowledge without right conduct is useless’; the original context is failure to follow revelation, not covetousness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And thou shalt take no gift: for the gift blindeth the wise, and perverteth the words of the righteous.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids judges to take bribes because the desire for gain blinds even wise people.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts warn that desire for another’s wealth disables even the sharpest mind.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Strong match (gain blinding the wise); the specific context is judicial bribery.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “To his own ruin the fool gains knowledge, for it cleaves his head and destroys his innate goodness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that knowledge in the hands of someone without virtue works against him and destroys his goodness.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts insist that intelligence alone cannot save someone whose conduct is bad.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Shares the ‘knowledge becomes useless or harmful without virtue’ idea; coveting is not named.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Erysichthon, wanting timber for his banquet hall, cut down Demeter’s sacred grove despite every warning. Demeter cursed him with insatiable hunger; he devoured his fortune, sold his own daughter, and at last consumed his own body.
greek_mythology.explanation: A king with every advantage let greed for what was sacred and not his drive him into total madness and self-destruction.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Erysichthon shows the Kural’s veriya (senseless) conduct: greed turns a powerful man’s judgment into madness.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Good on greed producing senseless self-destruction; the myth does not stress the loss of learning or intellect specifically.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s account of the oligarchic man, the money-loving part of the soul is set on the throne, and reason is made to sit at its feet, permitted only to calculate how more money can be made.
philosophy.explanation: Plato describes a person whose intelligence is still working but is now just a servant of his desire for wealth.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s diagnosis precisely: a sharp, wide intellect made worthless by covetousness.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the passage. Excellent conceptual match (reason enslaved to acquisitiveness).

kurals.tamil:
அருள்வெஃகி ஆற்றின்கண் நின்றான் பொருள்வெஃகிப்
பொல்லாத சூழக் கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Arulvehki aatrinkan nindraan porulvehkip
Pollaadha soozhak kedum.
kurals.meaning: Even a person who has longed for grace and stood firmly on the path of virtue will be ruined if he starts coveting others’ wealth and plotting wicked ways to get it.
kurals.elementary: Think of a kid who has always been kind and helpful. If one day they start scheming to take someone else’s things, all that goodness can come crashing down. This kural says no one is so good that greed can’t ruin them.
kurals.university: The kural turns on a deliberate repetition: the same verb வெஃகு (vehku, ‘to desire’) is used for the noble desire for அருள் (arul, grace/compassion) and the base desire for பொருள் (porul, wealth). The same faculty of longing can be aimed upward or downward, and a person who has aimed it well can still redirect it disastrously. ஆற்றின்கண் நின்றான் (aatrinkan nindraan, ‘one who stood in the path’) is read by Parimelazhagar as the householder’s path by which grace is attained, and more broadly by modern commentators as the path of virtue; பொல்லாத சூழ (pollaadha soozha) stresses that plotting is itself ruinous, even before any theft. The kural is a warning against spiritual complacency, echoed in the Gita’s admission that the senses carry away even a striving sage, and in the Qur’anic portrait of the man raised by signs who ‘adhered to the earth’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The senses are so strong and impetuous, O Arjuna, that they forcibly carry away the mind even of a man of discrimination who is endeavoring to control them.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns that even a wise person who is actively striving can be carried off by desire.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural warns the same: one who has stood on the path of grace can still be ruined by desire for wealth.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Strong on ‘even the striving virtuous can fall to desire’; the object is sense-desire generally rather than others’ wealth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says that some who were once in the faith coveted money, wandered away, and brought great pain on themselves.
christianity.tie_back: An almost exact parallel: people already on the path of faith were ruined by coveting.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Near one-to-one: those on the path of faith fall away through coveting and are ruined.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if We had willed, we could have elevated him thereby, but he adhered [instead] to the earth and followed his own desire. So his example is like that of the dog: if you chase him, he pants, or if you leave him, he [still] pants.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells of a man who had been given God’s signs and could have been raised high by them, but he clung to worldly things and followed his desire.
islam.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s fallen seeker: someone given grace who throws it away for worldly desire.
islam.source: Qur’an 7:176 (Sahih International; the account begins at 7:175)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (7:176). Strong structural match; ‘the earth’ and ‘desire’ are broader than coveting others’ wealth specifically.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the man of God, said, Behold, my master hath spared Naaman this Syrian, in not receiving at his hands that which he brought: but, as the LORD liveth, I will run after him, and take somewhat of him.”
judaism.explanation: Gehazi, the servant of the prophet Elisha, schemed to get the gifts his master had refused, lied to cover it, and was struck with leprosy (2 Kings 5:27).
judaism.tie_back: Gehazi lived in a prophet’s household (on the path of grace), coveted another’s wealth, plotted deceit to get it, and was ruined, just as the Kural describes.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (5:20 quoted). Near-perfect narrative match: a servant of a holy man covets, schemes, and is destroyed.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is one who, turning away from desire (for household life) takes to the life of the forest (i.e., of a monk). But after being freed from the household, he runs back to it. Behold that man! Though freed, he runs back to that very bondage!”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes someone who had renounced worldly desire but then ran back to it.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes the person already on the path who returns to worldly desire and loses what was gained.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Good on falling back from the path; about household attachment generally rather than coveting another’s wealth.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Tantalus, so favoured by the gods that he dined at their table, stole their nectar and ambrosia to share with mortals, and was cast down to eternal punishment in the underworld.
greek_mythology.explanation: Someone admitted to the gods’ own company threw it all away by taking what was not his.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s seeker who stood on the path of grace, Tantalus had divine favour and lost it through coveting and theft.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Pindar gives the theft of nectar and ambrosia as Tantalus’ crime (other versions differ); good narrative parallel of a favoured one falling through appropriation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the myth of the Ring of Gyges, a shepherd who finds a ring of invisibility uses it to seduce the queen, kill the king, and seize the kingdom. Glaucon argues that even a supposedly just man would do the same if he could act with impunity.
philosophy.explanation: Plato uses the story to ask whether anyone’s goodness would survive the chance to take whatever they wanted without consequence.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural answers Glaucon’s challenge: even the person who seemed to stand on the path will be ruined if he lets covetousness plot for him.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Addresses whether apparent virtue survives covetous opportunity; Plato uses it to test justice rather than to warn the pious.

kurals.tamil:
வேண்டற்க வெஃகியாம் ஆக்கம் விளைவயின்
மாண்டற் கரிதாம் பயன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vendarka vehkiyaam aakkam vilaivayin
Maandar karithaam payan.
kurals.meaning: Do not wish for prosperity that comes from coveting others’ goods; when it finally ripens, its fruit will rarely turn out to be good.
kurals.elementary: It’s like planting a seed you stole from your neighbour’s garden. It might grow, but the fruit tastes bitter because you know how you got it. This kural says wealth you got by grabbing others’ things never gives you a truly good harvest.
kurals.university: The kural uses an agricultural metaphor: வெஃகியாம் ஆக்கம் (vehkiyaam aakkam, ‘increase that comes through coveting’) is a crop, and விளைவயின் (vilaivayin, ‘at the time of its ripening’) its fruit is மாண்டற்கு அரிது (maandarku arithu, ‘hard to be excellent’). The argument concerns delayed consequences: ill-gotten gain may look like prosperity at first, but its maturation reveals its true nature. Some commentators (e.g., Solomon Pappaiah) read maandal as ‘goodness’ in enjoyment, while others read it as ‘glory’; either way the gain proves hollow. The theme of sweet-at-first, bitter-at-the-end fruit links this kural to the Gita’s account of rajasic happiness and to Proverbs’ ‘bread of deceit.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That happiness which is derived from contact of the senses with their objects and which appears like nectar at first but poison at the end is said to be of the nature of passion.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes pleasures of passion (rajas) as sweet at first but poisonous once they have run their course.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural says the same of covetous gain: it looks good at first, but its ripened fruit is bad.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Strong on the nectar-then-poison maturation structure; the object is sense-pleasure generally, not covetous gain specifically.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided? So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus’ parable, a rich man plans bigger barns for his harvest, but he dies that night and never enjoys any of it.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it warns that gain pursued through greed does not bear good fruit when the time comes.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Matches ‘greedy gain yields no lasting good’; the rich fool is greedy but not a coveter of others’ property.

islam.quote_or_event: “O Hakim! This property is like a sweet fresh fruit; whoever takes it without greediness, he is blessed in it, and whoever takes it with greediness, he is not blessed in it, and he is like a person who eats but is never satisfied.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet tells Hakim ibn Hizam that wealth taken with greed carries no blessing and never satisfies.
islam.tie_back: Almost the same image as the Kural: wealth is a fruit, and when greed is how you get it, the fruit is not good.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (sunnah.com English). Near one-to-one, including the fruit metaphor and the ‘no blessing’ outcome.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Bread of deceit is sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs says that what you gain dishonestly tastes sweet at first but later turns to gravel in your mouth.
judaism.tie_back: The same arc as the Kural’s ripened fruit: sweet at first, bad when it matures.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Very close structural match (ill-gotten gain, sweet then bitter).

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is no satisfying sensual desires, even with the rain of gold coins. For sensual pleasures give little satisfaction and much pain.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says even a rain of gold could not satisfy desire, and what it brings is more pain than pleasure.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says gain chased by craving yields little good and much harm.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (excerpted). Matches the ‘craving’s fruit is pain’ idea; not specifically about others’ property.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas asked Dionysus that everything he touched should turn to gold. His wish was granted, but his bread and wine turned to metal as he tried to eat, and he begged the god to take the gift back.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas got exactly the riches he craved, and they turned out to be useless, even deadly.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s point in myth: greedy gain, once it ‘ripens’, gives no good fruit.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Strong on greedy gain proving worthless; Midas does not covet another’s property but boundless wealth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes those who take gain from shameful sources, such as petty extortion or exploiting others, as displaying ‘sordid love of gain’ (aischrokerdeia): they endure reproach for the sake of gain, and small gain at that.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says that people who profit dishonourably earn disgrace, not honour, and the profit is small anyway.
philosophy.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s maandarku arithu: such gain rarely yields anything excellent or honourable.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Good match on shameful gain bringing reproach rather than excellence; the ripening metaphor is absent.

kurals.tamil:
அஃகாமை செல்வத்திற்கு யாதெனின் வெஃகாமை
வேண்டும் பிறன்கைப் பொருள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ahkaamai selvaththirku yaadhenin vehkaamai
Vendum pirankaip porul.
kurals.meaning: If you ask what keeps one’s wealth from dwindling, the answer is this: do not covet the property in another person’s hands.
kurals.elementary: If you want to keep your own toys safe, the best rule is never to grab other people’s toys. Then no one has a reason to take yours, and you stay happy with what you have. This kural says not wanting other people’s things is the secret to keeping your own.
kurals.university: The kural is built on a pun that is lost in translation: அஃகாமை (ahkaamai, ‘non-diminishing’) and வெஃகாமை (vehkaamai, ‘non-coveting’) differ by a single consonant, so the grammar of the line enacts its claim that the one secures the other. It is framed as a riddle with its own answer (‘yaadhenin…’, ‘if one asks what…’), a didactic device Valluvar uses often. பிறன் கைப் பொருள் (piran kaip porul, ‘property in another’s hand’) pointedly includes even possessions casually within reach. The ethical logic is both moral and practical: a society in which people do not covet is one in which everyone’s wealth is secure, and a mind that does not covet does not feel its own wealth as insufficient. The kural thus unites the tenth commandment’s social function with the Upanishadic ‘do not covet’ as a spiritual discipline.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “ALL this, whatsoever moves on earth, is to be hidden in the Lord (the Self). When thou hast surrendered all this, then thou mayest enjoy. Do not covet the wealth of any man!”
hinduism.explanation: The Isha Upanishad’s first verse says everything belongs to the Lord; enjoy what is given in that spirit, and do not covet anyone’s wealth.
hinduism.tie_back: ‘Do not covet the wealth of any man’ is the Kural’s vehkaamai in the Upanishad’s own words, presented as the basis of rightful enjoyment.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (Müller, SBE 1). Near one-to-one on ‘do not covet another’s wealth’, linked to rightful enjoyment of one’s own.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews tells believers to live free of covetousness and be content, because God will never abandon them.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ties freedom from coveting to the security of what one has.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Good match on non-covetousness plus security; the guarantee is divine presence rather than undiminished wealth.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not wish for that by which Allah has made some of you exceed others. For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women is a share of what they have earned. And ask Allah of his bounty.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says not to long for what others have been given, but to keep to your own earned share and ask God for more.
islam.tie_back: Same prescription as the Kural: don’t desire what is in another’s hand; your own share is secure.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Strong match on not coveting others’ portion; the ‘keeps wealth from diminishing’ element is implicit.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour’s.”
judaism.explanation: The tenth commandment (lo tachmod) forbids even the inner desire for anything that belongs to one’s neighbour.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Any thing that is thy neighbour’s’ is the Kural’s piran kaip porul, the property in another’s hand.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Near-identical prohibition; the commandment does not give the Kural’s rationale (preservation of one’s own wealth).

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ever grows the glory of him who is energetic, mindful and pure in conduct, discerning and self-controlled, righteous and heedful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says the fortune of a person of pure, self-controlled, righteous conduct keeps increasing.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it links pure, restrained conduct to prosperity that does not decline.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Shares the ‘virtue sustains prosperity’ link; ‘glory’ is broader than wealth and non-covetousness is not named.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In his elegy to the Muses, Solon prays for wealth but refuses to acquire it unjustly: wealth the gods give stays with a man secure from bottom to top, while wealth men chase through outrage (hubris) comes unwillingly and is soon mixed with ruin.
greek_mythology.explanation: Solon says that justly gained wealth lasts, while wealth gained by overreaching brings destruction.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Same claim as the Kural: not grasping at what is not yours is what keeps your wealth from dwindling.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the elegy (not quoted verbatim). Strong match on just-versus-unjust wealth and its durability.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Is anything brought around to you? Put out your hand and take your share with moderation. Does it pass by you? Don’t stop it. Is it not yet come? Don’t stretch your desire towards it, but wait till it reaches you. Do this with regard to children, to a wife, to public posts, to riches…”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus compares life to a dinner party: take your own portion politely and don’t reach for dishes that belong to others or haven’t come to you yet.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s rule in Stoic form: do not reach for what is in another’s hand.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (MIT Classics, Carter). Strong on non-grasping; the promised reward is fitness for the feasts of the gods, not undiminished wealth.

kurals.tamil:
அறனறிந்து வெஃகா அறிவுடையார்ச் சேரும்
திறன்அறிந் தாங்கே திரு.
kurals.transliteration:
Aranarindhu vehkaa arivudaiyaarch serum
Thiranarin thaange thiru.
kurals.meaning: Fortune, the goddess Thiru, recognises the worth of the wise who understand virtue and do not covet others’ goods, and she comes to them on her own accord, finding her way to them.
kurals.elementary: Imagine good luck as a friend who likes visiting kind, honest people. This kural says if you know what’s right and don’t try to take other people’s things, good fortune will find its way to your door by itself.
kurals.university: திரு (thiru), glossed by all traditional commentators as Lakshmi (Thirumagal), the goddess of fortune, is here personified as an agent with judgment: திறன் அறிந்து (thiran arindhu) means she ‘knows the proper way’ or ‘recognises their merit’ and arrives ஆங்கே (aange, ‘right there’). The kural thus reverses the covetous logic: the coveter reaches for wealth and loses it, while the one who does not reach is sought out by wealth itself. Parimelazhagar’s gloss emphasises that these people are அறிவுடையார் (arivudaiyaar) who know aram, so their restraint is a considered moral choice, not mere passivity. The idea that virtue attracts prosperity has close analogues in the Gita’s closing verse (where ‘sri’ accompanies righteousness), Socrates’ ‘from virtue come money and every other good’, and the Buddhist teaching that the righteous non-coveter may reappear among those of ‘great property’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Wherever there is Krsna, the master of all mystics, and wherever there is Arjuna, the supreme archer, there will also certainly be opulence, victory, extraordinary power, and morality.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita ends with Sanjaya declaring that where righteousness is, there Sri (fortune) will be too.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say Sri, fortune, goes to the side of righteousness; the Gita even uses the same goddess-word.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Shares the ‘Sri follows the righteous’ idea; non-covetousness is not specifically mentioned.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his listeners to seek righteousness first rather than chase material things, and those things will be given to them.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s reversal: don’t grasp at wealth, pursue virtue, and provision will come to you.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Very close structural match (seek righteousness, and material goods follow unbidden).

islam.quote_or_event: “And will provide for him from where he does not expect. And whoever relies upon Allah - then He is sufficient for him.”
islam.explanation: Continuing 65:2 (‘whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out’), the Qur’an promises that the God-conscious will be provided for from unexpected sources.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, provision comes to the righteous of its own accord rather than through their grasping.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (65:3). Good match on unsought provision for the righteous; non-coveting is implied by reliance rather than stated.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The blessing of the LORD, it maketh rich, and he addeth no sorrow with it.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs says real wealth comes from God’s blessing, and that kind of wealth carries no sorrow with it.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts say prosperity is given to the righteous rather than seized by them.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Matches ‘fortune comes as gift, not grab’; non-coveting and wisdom are not specified.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Here someone is not covetous: he is not a coveter of another’s chattels and property thus: ‘Oh, that what is another’s were mine!’” … “If a householder who observes conduct in accordance with the Dhamma, righteous conduct, should wish: ‘Oh, that … I might reappear in the company of the warrior-nobles of great property!’ it is possible…”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names non-covetousness as part of righteous conduct and says such a righteous householder can gain rebirth among people of great wealth.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s pairing: the one who does not covet another’s property is the one to whom prosperity comes.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (Access to Insight). Strong match: explicit non-covetousness linked to prosperity; the Buddhist frame is future rebirth rather than this life.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, a poor elderly couple, gladly shared their meagre food with disguised gods whom richer neighbours had turned away. Zeus and Hermes turned their hut into a temple, made them its priests, and granted their wish to die together.
greek_mythology.explanation: A poor couple who didn’t grasp at anything, and shared what little they had, were richly rewarded by the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s Thiru, divine favour sought out the humble and virtuous rather than those who grasped.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Good on fortune coming unbidden to the virtuous poor; the story centres on hospitality rather than non-covetousness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I tell you that virtue is not given by money, but that from virtue come money and every other good of man, public as well as private.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates says virtue doesn’t come from wealth; it is the other way round, and every good, including wealth, comes from virtue.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s claim in philosophical form: virtue comes first, and fortune follows it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (MIT Classics, Jowett). Strong match on ‘wealth follows virtue’; non-covetousness is not named.

kurals.tamil:
இறலீனும் எண்ணாது வெஃகின் விறல்ஈனும்
வேண்டாமை என்னுஞ் செருக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Iraleenum ennaadhu vehkin viraleenum
Vendaamai ennum serukku.
kurals.meaning: Coveting others’ property without thinking of the consequences gives birth to destruction; the proud strength of simply not wanting gives birth to victory.
kurals.elementary: Grabbing for something that isn’t yours without thinking is like reaching into a fire: you get burned. But being strong enough to say “I don’t need that” is like winning a race. This kural says not wanting is a kind of superpower.
kurals.university: The chapter closes with a perfectly balanced antithesis built on a rhyme: இறல் ஈனும் (iral eenum, ‘gives birth to destruction’) against விறல் ஈனும் (viral eenum, ‘gives birth to victory’). The verb ஈன் (een, ‘to bear, as offspring’) makes both outcomes the natural children of their causes. எண்ணாது (ennaadhu, ‘without reflecting’) identifies thoughtlessness about consequences as the root of covetousness, while வேண்டாமை என்னும் செருக்கு (vendaamai ennum serukku) calls non-desire a kind of செருக்கு (serukku, ‘pride, exaltation, greatness’). Valluvar reclaims a word usually negative and makes it the dignity of the person who needs nothing from others. The idea that restraint is itself a victory appears in Epictetus, in the Qur’anic promise of success to those saved from their own avarice, and in the Buddhist ‘craving-freed’ who vanquishes all suffering.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There are three gates leading to this hell-lust, anger, and greed. Every sane man should give these up, for they lead to the degradation of the soul.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names greed (lobha) as one of three gates to self-destruction and says every sensible person should abandon it.
hinduism.tie_back: Matches the destructive half of the Kural (iral eenum): unreflective greed gives birth to ruin.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Strong on greed-to-destruction; the victory half of the antithesis is not stated.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But godliness with contentment is great gain.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says the real profit in life is godliness combined with contentment.
christianity.tie_back: The positive half of the Kural: not wanting is itself a gain and a victory. The surrounding verses (6:9-10) supply the destructive half.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Strong on non-desire as ‘great gain’; read with 6:9-10 the passage covers both halves of the antithesis.

islam.quote_or_event: “…and find not any want in their breasts of what the emigrants were given but give [them] preference over themselves, even though they are in privation. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul - it is those who will be the successful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises the people of Madinah who felt no craving for what others received, and says those protected from their own greed (shuhh) are the successful ones.
islam.tie_back: Close to the Kural’s viral eenum: freedom from inner craving is what yields success and victory.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (excerpted). Strong match: no desire for what others were given, paired with ‘the successful’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that hasteth to be rich hath an evil eye, and considereth not that poverty shall come upon him.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs says someone in a greedy rush to get rich doesn’t stop to consider that it will bring him to ruin.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s ennaadhu (without thinking) is Proverbs’ ‘considereth not’; both say thoughtless greed leads to ruin.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Close match on thoughtless covetousness leading to ruin; the victory half is absent.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The gift of Dhamma excels all gifts; the taste of the Dhamma excels all tastes; the delight in Dhamma excels all delights. The Craving-Freed vanquishes all suffering.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says the person free of craving conquers all suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: Victory through non-desire: the Buddhist version of the Kural’s viral eenum vendaamai.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim. Strong on non-craving as victory; the ‘destruction’ half is found in neighbouring verse 355.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “…as often happens when gain deceives men’s sense and dishonour tramples down honour, the gods soon blot him out and make that man’s house low, and wealth attends him only for a little time.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns that a man who seizes wealth when greed clouds his judgment is soon destroyed by the gods, and the wealth doesn’t last.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s iral eenum ennaadhu vehkin: coveting without thought brings destruction.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (excerpted from Theoi text). Strong on thoughtless greed leading to destruction; the passage also opens ‘god-given wealth is much better’, loosely paralleling the victory half.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “…bring to your mind both points of time: that in which you will enjoy the pleasure, and that in which you will repent and reproach yourself after you have enjoyed it; and set before you, in opposition to these, how you will be glad and applaud yourself if you abstain … how much better it is to be conscious of having gained so great a victory.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus advises weighing what comes after giving in to a desire against the joy of holding back, and calls holding back a great victory.
philosophy.tie_back: Both halves of the Kural: think of the consequences (the opposite of ennaadhu), and see that abstaining is a victory (viral).
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (excerpted; MIT Classics, Carter). Close match on reflecting on consequences and abstention as ‘victory’; concerns pleasure generally rather than others’ property.
